transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Kim (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood), Alan Park (CTO, Verdant), Sara Cho (ML Lead), Daniel Ortega (Infra), Maya Li (Product)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focused on prefix/prompt caching strategy, how tokenization choices affect KV cache hit rates, eviction policies for multi-tenant safety, and tradeoffs with quantized models and batching under a VPC/private deployment. Action items and pilot next steps agreed.

Topics (auto):
- Tokenization boundary sensitivity and prefix stability
- Cache key design (normalized prompts, metadata tags)
- Hotset vs hotcache eviction simulations
- Quantization and KV size tradeoffs
- Batching and latency SLOs in private runtime

[00:00] Jenna: hey everyone thanks for joining. can we do quick intros?
[00:05] Alan: yeah alan here, CTO at Verdant. we run a customer-facing assistant, highly prefix-sensitive prompts, lots of identical opening system messages.
[00:12] Sara: sara, ml lead, i'm focused on quality — especially when responses vary by tokenization.
[00:17] Daniel: daniel infra, responsible for private cloud and VPC peering.
[00:21] Jenna: great. marco on the call?
[00:24] Marco: yep marco ruiz, se — i'll lead the technical bits on kv, batching and kernel/quant notes.
[00:29] Maya: maya, product — will be shepherding success criteria.

[00:45] Marco: ok quick agenda: first we examine tokenization and how small changes in the prefix --- like a trailing space or punctuation --- can break cache hits; then key normalization, deduping, tenant tags; eviction policies for shared cache; and finally how quantization increases kv size and affects throughput, and recommendations for the private pilot.

[01:12] Alan: our main worry is correctness — if a cached continuation is wrong for one tenant or prompt variant, that's a showstopper. cost and latency matter but safety first.

[02:05] Marco: totally, so two prongs: 1) improve hit-rate without loosening semantic correctness, and 2) isolate tenants and provide safe fallback.

[03:00] Sara: quick note: our prompts often include user metadata embedded in the system prompt, like "User: <firstName>" which changes every request. so naive full-prompt keys are useless.

[03:17] Marco: yep that's classic. we recommend building a normalized key blueprint: strip or hash ephemeral user fields, canonicalize whitespace, run deterministic tokenization, and optionally include a small sketch of the last N tokens (e.g., 32-token signature) rather than the full prompt. that keeps keys compact and improves hit rates.

[04:02] Daniel: does Redwood provide tokenizer determinism across hosted/dedicated/private? we cannot have different tokenizers in prod vs pilot.

[04:12] Priya: good question — runtime includes a reproducible tokenizer binary; we ship the same tokenizer artifacts to private. but note, quantized kernels may alter subword segmentation slightly if model variant differs. we recommend pinning model versions and tokenizer hash.

[04:40] Sara: wait slight differences in segmentation? i thought tokenizers are deterministic.

[04:47] Marco: generally deterministic, but when you use different model checkpoints (even quantized variants) the vocabulary or merge rules sometimes change in edge cases. and some tooling pipelines re-normalize punctuation differently. best practice: pin both model hash and tokenizer hash in the key.

[05:10] Alan: ok that adds operational overhead but seems necessary. what about using token-level prefixes (kv cache keyed directly by token ids) vs string keys?

[05:23] Marco: token-id keys are more stable across whitespace but can be large; we usually hash the token id sequence to a fixed-length signature. collision risk is low with 128-bit hash but you still need to tag by tenant and model-variant to avoid cross-tenant leakage.

[06:00] Maya: can you give expected hit-rate uplifts with normalization? we ran a simple analysis and saw ~3-4x difference depending on user field variance.

[06:15] Marco: sure, in our internal datasets normalizing ephemeral fields and canonicalizing formatting bumped hit-rates from ~6% to ~28% on chat-ish workloads where system prompts are stable. with token-signature strategies we saw up to ~45% for very templated prefixes. your mileage will vary.

[07:00] Sara: that's promising. are there tradeoffs with freshness? if we normalize too much we might accidentally serve stale context when the ephemeral user variable actually meaningfully changes the expected continuation.

[07:14] Marco: yep that's why we suggest multi-tier keys: a strict key (exact prompt hashed) for conservative correctness; a relaxed key (normalized sketch) that is only used when a confidence filter passes — e.g., semantic similarity score between the new prompt and the cached prompt above a threshold. When in doubt, fall back to live generation.

[08:10] Alan: how do you compute that semantic similarity cheaply? can't run an embed per request.

[08:18] Marco: two techniques: 1) use cheap fingerprinting Hj/MinHash on normalized tokens for a quick similarity estimate, or 2) precompute embeddings for canonical prompt families and tag keys with family ids. embeddings add cost but are amortizable for stable families.

[09:05] Daniel: on eviction policies for a shared KV store: we will be multi-tenant and resource constrained in initial pilot. how do you avoid one tenant's hotset overrunning others?

[09:20] Marco: use tenant-aware quotas and weighted LRU. i.e., maintain per-tenant token budget and global budget. when global pressure increases, evict from tenants over their pro-rata share first. also keep a cold-reserve for spikes to ensure tail latency.

[10:10] Priya: we also recommend time-decayed hotness metric: hits decay over time so short-lived spikes don't permanently dominate the cache.

[11:00] Sara: ok about safety — what if a relaxed-key hit leaks user-specific instructions?

[11:08] Marco: that's the big one. never apply relaxed-key hits to prompts that contain PII or user-specific instructions (e.g., "do not share" or legal texts). Use prompt classifiers (fast regex or small model) to tag prompts as sensitive; sensitive prompts go through strict-key path only.

[11:45] Alan: can we tag tenant and content-sensitivity flags in our app before calling Redwood? we'd prefer app-level hints.

[11:53] Jenna: absolutely — API supports hints like x-prefix-safety: sensitive|non-sensitive and tenant_id. those are used in key generation.

[12:20] Maya: walk us through a concrete example: user asks the assistant which plan to pick, the system prompt contains product mappings. how does the cache key look?

[12:35] Marco: simplified: key = hash(model_hash + tokenizer_hash + tenant_id + family_id + sketch32 + sensitivity_flag). where sketch32 is hashed last-32 tokens signature. If the incoming prompt differs only in user name, sketch matches and we may hit the relaxed key; if the user instruction changes, sketch diverges and only strict-key path applies.

[13:40] Sara: what about tokenization edge cases, like emoji, zero-width joiners? we saw mismatched token boundaries causing cache misses.

[14:00] Marco: those are common. recommended: normalize unicode (NFKC), replace or canonicalize emoji sequences to stable placeholders before tokenization, and log mismatches in an observability pipeline so we can iteratively expand normalization rules.

[14:50] Alan: can the Redwood runtime apply those normalizations server-side? we'd rather not change client code for a pilot.

[15:00] Priya: yes, we can offer optional server-side normalization layers but we flag changes in a compatibility report. for strict compliance you should test locally because normalization can slightly alter semantics.

[16:30] Daniel: moving to quantization: what are the practical kv-size differences when serving 8-bit vs 4-bit quantized variants?

[16:42] Marco: KV cache is mostly floating-point key/value pairs for attention caches. quantized models often reduce KV memory footprint — 8-bit can cut memory by ~2x vs fp16, 4-bit more but at cost of compute overhead to dequantize. However, quantization can change tokenization consistency if the model variant differs, so pin model hash.

[17:30] Sara: note: our primary production is sensitive to subtle generation differences — are quality regressions from 4-bit an issue?

[17:45] Marco: many teams see minor quality delta for completion tasks but it's model-dependent. recommended approach: run a side-by-side A/B run with your canonical prompts. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload; for prefix-heavy workloads you might keep fp16 for critical families and use quantized for lower-priority routes.

[18:40] Maya: how does caching interact with quantization in terms of performance?

[18:50] Marco: caching reduces kernel calls; if your KV is warm, quantization overhead matters less because you skip full forward compute. but when cache misses spike, quantized backends may have higher latency due to dequantize steps — depends on kernel implementation and hardware. we include kernel-level benchmarks in the pilot.

[19:40] Alan: we run on-prem racks with A100-ish hardware. will Redwood's private runtime run optimized kernels or will we need to compile?

[19:50] Priya: private runtime ships with precompiled kernels for popular hardware (A100, H100 families). if you're on slightly older GPUs we may need a quick compile step; we give CI scripts to prebuild.

[20:25] Daniel: firewall/peering question: for private control plane + local runtime how do we handle KV metrics and audit logs — do logs leave our VPC?

[20:35] Jenna: logs are configurable: you can keep audit logs entirely on your side in Private mode, or ship summaries to Redwood for support. we also support local KMS and HSM integration.

[21:10] Sara: about batching: we have a mixture of interactive and batch flows. what batching strategies preserve our 200ms p95 interactive SLO while reducing cost for background tasks?

[21:22] Marco: continuous batching with latency targets is the sweet spot: maintain a small warm pool for interactive (no batching or micro-batches) and a separate pooled path for batch requests with higher latency allowance. Redwood runtime supports per-route batching policies and burst lanes for interactive traffic.

[22:05] Maya: any recommended numbers for micro-batching thresholds?

[22:12] Marco: for 200ms p95 interactive you want micro-batch windows ~1-3ms with prefetched KV; for background flows you can batch up to 16-32 tokens per request and window 10-50ms depending on traffic. these are workload-specific so we'll run tuning in the pilot.

[23:00] Alan: can we throttle specific tenants if they produce noisy huge prefixes?

[23:08] Marco: yes that's part of tenant-aware QoS: rate limits, token budgets, and dynamic throttles. we can apply soft-limits first and escalate to hard-limits if abuse observed.

[23:40] Sara: observability — we need to see per-key hit rate distributions and failure modes. what instrumentation does Redwood provide?

[23:48] Marco: per-tenant and per-route metrics: key-hit-rate, average prefix-length, eviction-rate, tail latency, model-variant diffs. we can stream metrics to your Prometheus, and there's also a console view with timelines. we also provide sampled transcripts and a mismatch detector for normalization failures.

[24:30] Maya: do you keep actual prompt text in logs? privacy is a no-go for us.

[24:37] Jenna: logs can be tokenized-only or hashed-only. we support PII redaction and local-only logging. all options documented in our security pack.

[25:00] Alan: what's the plan for the pilot and what success metrics should we set?

[25:10] Marco: pilot plan suggestion: 1) run 48-hour synthetic hotset run with your canonical prompts to exercise cache hit behavior; 2) run a shadow production replay for 1 week; 3) A/B a quantized variant on a subset of low-risk routes. Success metrics: p95 latency <=200ms for interactive, hit-rate uplift >=20% for targeted families, no cross-tenant leakage (0 incidents), and cost-per-1000 tokens reduced by >=15% on pilot routes.

[26:05] Daniel: can you provide the synthetic harness?

[26:10] Jenna: yes will share harness link and a docker image.

[27:00] Sara: another concern: collision risk with hashed signatures — is 128-bit enough?

[27:08] Marco: 128-bit collision is astronomically unlikely for your volumes, but we also keep a per-entry nonce and tenant tag so collisions can't cross-tenant. collisions are also logged to the mismatch detector.

[27:45] Alan: curious about fallback policies — if a relaxed-key match occurs but downstream safety checks fail, do you have an automatic regeneration path?

[27:52] Marco: yes, the runtime will re-run generation on mismatch or safety fail and also optionally trigger a negative cache entry for that sketch to reduce subsequent wrong relax-hits for a small TTL.

[28:30] Maya: show of hands — any blockers on security side to run the pilot?

[28:36] Daniel: need SSO and SOC2 docs, plus proof-of-concept for KMS integration.

[28:42] Jenna: we'll attach the security pack and KMS integration guide in the follow-up.

[29:10] Sara: i want to dig into the data we saw earlier: an internal run showed certain prompt families with 60% miss despite being templated; we suspect unicode and punctuation variance. can you run an analysis?

[29:22] Marco: yes we'll run tokenization diff on your sample. please share a dump of ~5k prompt headers.

[30:05] Alan: cost modeling — how should we think about dedicated vs shared private deployment for this workload?

[30:17] Marco: depends on concurrency and tail-latency needs. dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable throughput and lower unit cost at high scale. private with shared pools + strong caching may be cost effective early on because caching reduces consumed GPU cycles, but dedicated is more predictable for high-traffic tenants. we'll provide a cost model spreadsheet that lets you plug in expected hit rates and concurrency.

[31:10] Priya: also include the impact of prefix cache hit-rate on token throughput: each hit saves a variable number of token decodes — we'll help estimate median saved tokens per family.

[32:05] Sara: curious about one more edge case: if a cached continuation was generated under an older instruction set (different system prompt) and now the system prompt changed, how do you prevent stale responses?

[32:20] Marco: include a system_prompt_hash in the key and an optional TTL per key that invalidates on prompt schema changes. plus we support a 'prompt versioning' header so app can indicate major changes.

[33:05] Alan: great. what's the expected turnaround for initial benchmark results?

[33:12] Jenna: we'll share the benchmark skeleton within 48 hours and run first synthetic results within a week.

[34:00] Maya: any other Redwood notes about multi-tenant safety?

[34:06] Marco: two-layer defense: engineering controls (tenant tags, quotas, per-tenant eviction) and runtime checks (sensitivity classifier, strict vs relaxed key paths). also maintain audit trails for any relaxed-key hits used to seed responses.

[35:00] Sara: one tangential question: do you recommend storing prefix sketches in a separate high-availability KV (in-memory) or co-located on disk-backed store?

[35:12] Marco: hot KV should be in-memory (RAM/NVMe-backed with persistence off) for latency. we also persist checkpointed cold snapshots to disk for warm-starts. persistent cold store reduces warmup time after restarts.

[36:00] Daniel: what are operational costs for keeping a larger in-memory KV? we have limited RAM budget on-prem.

[36:08] Marco: that's where eviction policies and hotset sizing matter. you can configure a hot-reserve per tenant and cap global memory. plus Redwood Optimize can recommend sketch size and TTLs to stay within given RAM budgets.

[37:10] Alan: do you have example TTLs you recommend?

[37:17] Marco: for highly templated families, TTLs of hours are fine; for conversational ephemeral data, minutes. hybrid approach: hotset with short TTL and a warm backup with longer TTL.

[38:00] Priya: quick comment on observability: we'll provide dashboards with per-key sample traces so you can replay the request that created cached entry. those traces are scrubbed unless you opt-in to store plaintext.

[39:00] Sara: ok i'm convinced. let's talk about the actual pilot steps and who's responsible.

[39:10] Jenna: pilot scope: 48h synthetic run + 1 week shadow replay + quantized A/B on 10% traffic for non-sensitive routes. deliverables: harness, cost model, kernels for your infra, and security docs.

[39:40] Daniel: we'll provision a staging VPC and run the peering; tentative window 2026-05-18 to 2026-05-25.

[40:05] Marco: we'll need a short access window for metrics export — can be read-only.

[40:20] Alan: how will we validate zero leakage? do you run a negative test?

[40:28] Marco: yes we can run cross-tenant synthetic tests designed to detect leakage and verify tenancy isolation.

[41:00] Maya: any legal considerations for logs?

[41:06] Jenna: we'll include the legal/process docs in the follow-up; but main point: you can opt to keep PII redaction and audit logs on-prem.

[41:40] Sara: earlier you mentioned sketch sizes. what's the sensible sketch-length for us?

[41:48] Marco: start with 32-token sketch and measure. for long system prompts maybe 64. smaller sketches reduce KV size but may lower hit fidelity.

[42:30] Alan: what about cache key entropy and partitioning? we want to avoid hot partitions on certain cache shards.

[42:39] Marco: consistent hashing with tenant-aware sharding. also use salted hashes per time-window to spread writes if you see a single tenant hotspot. avoid sequential key patterns.

[43:10] Daniel: deep ops question: what's the eviction coordination mechanism across a multi-node cluster?

[43:17] Marco: we use a distributed lease protocol to coordinate evictions and to avoid thundering herds. evictions are lazy and often executed by local nodes first; global rebalancing runs asynchronously.

[44:05] Sara: any recommended instrumentation to detect repeated misses for the same family?

[44:12] Marco: yes an alert for family-miss-rate > threshold and repeated normalization mismatches. we can attach auto-tickets to your issue tracker if you want.

[45:00] Maya: quick question about compiled kernels: how long is typical compile time for custom hardware?

[45:06] Marco: usually minutes for common GPU types; rare architectures can take a few hours. we provide parallel compile infra.

[45:45] Alan: ok let's reiterate next steps so we have clear assignees.

[45:52] Jenna: recap: Jenna to share harness, cost model, security docs; Marco to run tokenization diffs and synthetic prefix warm/cold runs; Sara to provide prompt families; Daniel to provision staging VPC and share access window; all to reconvene after synthetic results.

[46:20] Sara: question — can the pilot include a short on-device test for offline inference? we have an edge node team.

[46:30] Marco: edge inference often needs smaller quantized models; caching strategies differ. we can scope that as a follow-up if you want.

[47:10] Alan: any gotchas you want to call out?

[47:16] Marco: main gotchas: 1) tokenization drift across environments, 2) relaxed-key safety false positives if sensitivity detection is off, 3) underestimated warm-up time after restarts if you don't persist warm snapshots.

[48:00] Priya: also note observability sampling rate — sample too little and you won't see rare mis-hits; sample too much and you leak privacy. configure carefully.

[48:45] Daniel: we'll review the security pack this week.

[49:05] Jenna: i'll send a follow-up with all links; also included is a short checklist for VPC peering and firewall ports.

[50:00] Marco: i'll kick off tokenization diffs once we get the prompt dump. expect initial notes in 3 business days.

[50:20] Maya: any final questions?

[50:25] Alan: none from me. thanks, very useful.

[50:30] Sara: thanks all.

[50:35] Jenna: thanks folks — we'll send notes and schedule the pilot kickoff.

Closing notes:
- Links to be shared: benchmark harness (docker + scripts), cost model spreadsheet, security pack, tokenizer diff tool, synthetic harness results template.
- Risk: normalization changes can affect semantics — recommended local verification.

Action items reiterated: see action_items field above.

End of transcript.
